281.title: Home to the porch
281.hook: after seven visits, a deeper look at the school this path quotes most
281.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism today often keep a short line from Epictetus, Seneca or Marcus Aurelius close by and reread it in the morning or when something goes wrong.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vaisakhi, the harvest and the founding of the Khalsa. Your line was a new beginning. What did you start? Day two hundred eighty-one.

Seven weeks. Seven doors. We sat in a Hindu home with a lamp and a flower, took refuge with Buddhists, argued over a page with Jewish students, walked with Christians and with Catholics, fasted with Muslims, and ate on the floor with Sikhs. Each time we were guests, and a good guest goes home. So where is home on this path? If you've walked this path from the start, you know. Think of the voice that argued with itself under the blankets, the enslaved teacher, the man who wrote letters about time. Today: home to the porch.
screen: `SEVEN WEEKS, SEVEN DOORS.` → `A GOOD GUEST GOES HOME.` → `HOME TO THE PORCH.`

segments.voice: Back on day twenty-seven we met the porch itself: the Stoa Poikile, the painted colonnade on the edge of the market in Athens, where a shipwrecked merchant named Zeno started teaching around 300 BCE. The school was named after the porch. Since then we've quoted three Romans more than anyone: Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius. So this month we go deeper, and it helps to know the shape of the whole school first. Stoics split philosophy into three parts: logic, how to think clearly; physics, how the world works; and ethics, how to live. Diogenes Laërtius, who collected their lives, reports that they liked to picture it as a fenced orchard. Logic is the fence. Physics is the soil and the trees. Ethics is the fruit. You can't have the fruit without the rest. Now the honest part. Almost everything the early Greek Stoics wrote is lost. Chrysippus, the school's great systematizer, is said to have written more than seven hundred books. Not one survives whole. What we have are fragments quoted by other people, often by critics. The Stoicism most of us know is the late Roman version, practical and personal, written by men who were trying to live it. So the next weeks go in order: first what the Stoics said is good, then how they saw feelings, then their picture of the world, and then the Stoics honestly, with their blind spots. Let's start where Epictetus starts his Handbook, in George Long's 1877 translation: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not."

segments.voice: Let's reread one line, slowly, the way you'd come back to a house you grew up in. Of things some are in our power, and others are not. Say it once in your head. Then let one thing from this week drift up. Which side of the line does it sit on? Don't fix it. Just notice where it lands. The bell holds the time.
Home to the porch. The painted porch in Athens that named the Stoics, the school this path quotes most, and where we return this month. Today's word.
Your line: home to the porch. Today, reread one Stoic line you remember, from any day on this path, and see if it lands differently now. Day two hundred eighty-one.

282.title: Character is the good
282.hook: for the Stoics only virtue is truly good, and health and money are extras
282.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often weigh a decision by asking what a person of good character would do, putting that above what they stand to gain or lose.

segments.voice: Yesterday we came home to the porch, the school this path quotes most. Which Stoic line did you reread? Day two hundred eighty-two.

Imagine a wish list for your life. Most of us could fill it in without thinking. Good health. Enough money, maybe more than enough. A decent job, people who like us, a nice place to live. Now imagine a philosopher reading your list over your shoulder and saying: those are fine. Pleasant, even. But not one of them is actually good. Only one thing is good, and it's not on your list. That's what the Stoics said, and they meant it. Today: arete, and the idea that character is the good.
screen: `HEALTH, MONEY, A GOOD JOB.` → `FINE, BUT NOT GOOD.` → `ARETE.`

segments.voice: Arete is Greek, and we usually translate it virtue. But the Greek word is wider and more practical. It means excellence, being good at what a thing is for. The arete of a knife is cutting well. The arete of a horse is running well. So what is a human being for? The Stoics answered: we're the animals that reason and live together. Our excellence is reasoning well and treating each other well. In a word, character. Then comes the bold claim. For the Stoics, character is the only thing that's truly good, and bad character the only thing that's truly bad. Here's their test. A good thing should be good for you in every situation; it can never be used badly. Money fails that test: it can buy a meal for a hungry friend or a bribe. Health fails it: a strong body can help a neighbor move or hurt someone. Even cleverness can be used for a con. But wisdom? Justice? Courage? The Stoics said these can't be turned to a bad use, because using things well is exactly what they are. Nobody does harm with too much justice. That's why Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius, keeps coming back to one idea: the only good is what is honorable, and a person is measured by that and nothing else. The Stoics weren't against health or money. Tomorrow and the day after, we'll see they gladly preferred them. But they wouldn't stake a life on them. If you lose your job and keep your honesty, the Stoic says you've lost something pleasant and kept the thing that matters. It's a demanding idea. It's also strangely freeing.
screen: `ARETE — EXCELLENCE, BEING GOOD AT IT.` · `A HUMAN'S JOB: REASON AND LIVE TOGETHER.` · `ONLY WHAT CAN'T BE USED BADLY IS GOOD.` · `LOSE THE JOB, KEEP THE HONESTY.` · then, large: `CHARACTER FIRST.`

segments.voice: Let three things you want from today come to mind. A task, a result, a feeling, anything. Line them up. Now ask of each one: is this about what I get, or about who I am while I get it? Maybe finish the report, and be honest in it. Move the character part to the top of the list. Sit with that order for a while. The bell holds the time.
Arete. Greek for excellence: being good at what you're for. For the Stoics, a human's excellence is good character, the only true good. Today's word.
Your line: character first. When you rank today's goals, put how you'll act above what you'll get, just once, and see what changes. Day two hundred eighty-two.

283.title: Four virtues
283.howItsDone: Modern Stoic practitioners often pick one of the four virtues as a focus for the day and review in the evening where it showed up or went missing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arete, excellence, and the Stoic claim that character is the only true good. Your line was character first. Did it change your list? Day two hundred eighty-three.

If character is the only good, the obvious next question is: what does good character look like? Not in a sermon. On a Wednesday. When the kid spills the juice, when the boss asks you to fudge a number, when the last slice of cake is looking at you. The Stoics didn't leave it vague. They had a short list, four words long, that they inherited from Plato and turned into a daily tool. You could fit it on a sticky note. Today: the four virtues.
screen: `WHAT DOES CHARACTER LOOK LIKE?` → `ON A WEDNESDAY.` → `FOUR WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here they are. Wisdom: seeing clearly what's good, what's bad and what doesn't matter, and knowing what to do. Courage: doing the right thing when it's frightening or uncomfortable, and bearing what has to be borne. Justice: treating people fairly and kindly, doing your part for the common good. And self-control, sometimes called temperance or moderation: wanting things in the right measure, not being dragged around by appetite. The Greek word for that last one is sophrosyne, literally something like a sound mind, a safe and healthy way of thinking. Plato had already named these four. Much later, Christian writers took them up as the cardinal virtues, from the Latin for a hinge, the virtues a good life swings on. Now the Stoic twist, and it's the part people forget. For the Stoics these aren't four separate skills you collect like badges. They're one excellence seen from four sides. You can't really have one without the others. Take courage without justice: a bold thief. Is that courage? The Stoics said no, that's just nerve. Or justice without wisdom: meaning well and making a mess. Self-control without courage: a careful coward. So each virtue needs the others to be itself. Marcus Aurelius, writing to himself, asks more than once whether he's found anything in life better than justice, truth, self-control and courage. He never did. That makes the list practical. In any moment, you can ask four questions: what's true here, what's brave, what's fair, and what's enough?
screen: `WISDOM, COURAGE, JUSTICE, SELF-CONTROL.` · `NAMED BY PLATO, KEPT BY MANY.` · `ONE EXCELLENCE, FOUR SIDES.` · `TRUE, BRAVE, FAIR, ENOUGH?` · then, large: `FOUR VIRTUES.`

segments.voice: Picture the rest of today, its meetings, meals, messages. Now hold up the four, one at a time. Wisdom. Courage. Justice. Self-control. Which one does today most need from you? Don't overthink it. The one that makes you wince a little is often the answer. Pick it. Say its name quietly on each out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Four virtues. Wisdom, courage, justice and self-control: for the Stoics, one good character seen from four sides. Today's word.
Your line: four virtues. Carry the one you picked. When a choice comes up, ask what it would look like here. Day two hundred eighty-three.

284.title: Nice, not needed
284.hook: Stoics prefer health and wealth but don't stake their happiness on them
284.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners enjoy comforts and pursue sensible goals like health and income, while reminding themselves that these are preferred, not necessary for a good life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four virtues, wisdom, courage, justice and self-control. Your line was four virtues. Which one did you carry, and where did it show up? Day two hundred eighty-four.

Two days ago the Stoics told us health and money aren't truly good. You might have thought: fine, easy to say from a marble bench. So does that mean a Stoic shrugs at a broken leg? Turns down a raise? Lives on cold water and gravel? No. And the reason is one of the cleverest ideas they had. It's about the difference between something you'd like and something you need. A warm coat on a cold day. A good night's sleep. A full fridge. Nice. Very nice. Today: adiaphora.
screen: `SO A STOIC SHRUGS AT A BROKEN LEG?` → `NO.` → `ADIAPHORA.`

segments.voice: Adiaphora is Greek for indifferents, things that don't make a difference. Not to your comfort; they make a big difference there. They make no difference to whether you're a good person. Health, wealth, reputation, even life itself: all indifferent in that one sense. But the Stoics sorted the indifferents. Some are preferred: health over sickness, enough money over poverty, friends over loneliness. It's natural and sensible to pick those, and a Stoic will. Others are dispreferred, and it's sensible to avoid them. Zeno explained the word preferred with a picture from a royal court, which Cicero passes on. At court, the ministers and nobles are promoted, placed near the throne. But none of them is the king. Health and money are like that: high in rank, never the ruler. Only character sits on the throne. Seneca, who was one of the richest men in Rome, liked this idea for obvious reasons, and his critics said so. His answer, in his essay On the Happy Life, is roughly: the wise person may own wealth, but wealth must not own him. Epictetus gives the gentlest picture of all, in his Handbook: behave in life as at a banquet. When a dish comes around to you, reach out and take a polite share. If it passes you by, don't grab at it. If it hasn't reached you yet, don't stretch across the table. Enjoy what's in front of you. Just don't stake your happiness on the next plate. That's the whole teaching in three words. Nice, not needed.
screen: `ADIAPHORA — INDIFFERENTS.` · `PREFERRED, AND DISPREFERRED.` · `NEAR THE THRONE, NEVER THE KING.` · `TAKE A SHARE AT THE BANQUET.` · then, large: `NICE, NOT NEEDED.`

segments.voice: Choose one comfort that's with you right now. The chair under you. A warm drink. The quiet in the room. Let yourself enjoy it fully for a few breaths. Really enjoy it. Then, gently, imagine it gone: the chair harder, the drink cold, the room loud. You'd still be you. Come back to the comfort, and hold it a little more lightly. The bell holds the time.
Adiaphora. Greek for indifferents: things like health and wealth that are worth preferring but don't make you good or bad. Today's word.
Your line: nice, not needed. Enjoy one comfort today, a good meal, a hot shower, a quiet minute, and hold it lightly, like a dish at the banquet. Day two hundred eighty-four.

285.title: Emotions as judgments
285.hook: Stoics saw destructive passions as mistaken judgments, not feeling itself
285.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners, and modern cognitive therapies influenced by them, look for the belief inside a strong emotion and ask whether it is accurate.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adiaphora, the indifferents, preferred but not needed. Your line was nice, not needed. Which comfort did you hold lightly? Day two hundred eighty-five.

Your friend doesn't text back. An hour. Three hours. By evening you're sure of it: they're annoyed with you, maybe finished with you. Your stomach is tight. Then the phone buzzes. Sorry, phone died, what's up? And the whole storm is gone in a second. Notice what just happened. Nothing changed in the world. The only thing that changed was the story you were telling yourself. The Stoics built a whole theory of emotion on moments like that one. Today: pathos.
screen: `NO TEXT BACK.` → `THE STORM, THEN THE BUZZ.` → `ONLY THE STORY CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Pathos is Greek, from a verb meaning to suffer, to undergo, to have something happen to you. It's where English gets passion, and pathetic, and sympathy. For the Stoics, a pathos was a passion in a narrow sense: a feeling that runs away with you, that you undergo instead of choose. They named four families: distress, fear, craving, and a kind of giddy, overexcited pleasure. Here's the surprising claim. Chrysippus, the great early Stoic, taught that these passions are judgments. Not the cause of a judgment, not a side effect. Inside every runaway feeling is a belief: something terrible has happened, or something terrible is coming, or I must have that, or this is the best thing ever. And very often the belief is false, or at least much too big. Epictetus says it plainly in his Handbook, in George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." Chrysippus had a picture for what a passion is like. When you walk, you can stop whenever you want. When you run downhill, your legs carry you past the point where you meant to stop. A passion is running downhill. Now, what the Stoics did not say: they didn't say all feeling is a mistake, or that you should become a stone. On the last day of this week we'll meet the good feelings they kept. What they said is that the destructive ones carry a hidden sentence. Find the sentence and you can check it. That's why the question matters so much: what am I telling myself?
screen: `PATHOS — SOMETHING YOU UNDERGO.` · `FOUR FAMILIES OF PASSION.` · `INSIDE EACH FEELING, A BELIEF.` · `RUNNING DOWNHILL.` · then, large: `WHAT AM I TELLING MYSELF?`

segments.voice: Bring up one feeling that's been with you today, even a small one. Irritation, worry, wanting. Let it be there. Now listen underneath it for the sentence. It usually starts with they, or I, or this. They don't respect me. I'm going to fail. This has to go well. Just find the sentence. Hold it up in the light. Is it true? Is it the whole truth? The bell holds the time.
Pathos. Greek for something you undergo: for the Stoics, a runaway passion built on a mistaken judgment. Today's word.
Your line: what am I telling myself. The next time a feeling grabs you today, ask it quietly, and see what sentence you find inside. Day two hundred eighty-five.

286.title: The first jolt
286.hook: Seneca: a jolt of shock isn't anger yet, agreeing with it is (On Anger 2.3)
286.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners treat a sudden flash of fear or anger as an involuntary first movement and pause before deciding whether to agree with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pathos, the runaway passion with a judgment hidden inside. Your line was what am I telling myself. What sentence did you find? Day two hundred eighty-six.

A ship in a storm, somewhere between Greece and Italy, in the second century. The Roman writer Aulus Gellius is on board, and so is a famous Stoic philosopher. The waves get huge. And the philosopher goes white as a sheet. When the storm passes, a rich passenger mocks him: some Stoic, you were as scared as the rest of us. The philosopher doesn't argue. He reaches into his bag, takes out a book of Epictetus, and shows Gellius a passage. It's about the first jolt.
screen: `A SHIP IN A STORM.` → `THE STOIC GOES WHITE.` → `SOME STOIC.`

segments.voice: Here's what the passage said, as Gellius retells it. When something frightening appears, even the mind of a wise person is shaken for a moment. It flinches, goes pale, jumps. That's not a failure. It's how a body works. What the wise person doesn't do is agree with it, doesn't go on to think: yes, this is truly terrible. The fool agrees, and adds more. Seneca laid out the same idea in his essay On Anger. He lists things nobody chooses: a shiver when cold water splashes you, dizziness at the edge of a cliff, a blush, the hair standing up on your arms at bad news. He calls these first movements. They happen to us. They are not yet anger, or fear. Anger, Seneca says, comes in a second step, when the mind signs off on the jolt: I've been wronged, and they should pay. Then there's a third step, when it's out of control and doesn't care whether it's right anymore. So picture three moments. The jolt. The yes. The runaway. The jolt isn't yours to stop. The yes is. This is a relief. It means a flash of anger in traffic, a stab of jealousy at a friend's good news, a lurch of panic at an email, isn't proof you're a bad person or a failed Stoic. It's weather passing through a body. You are the one who decides whether to agree with it. And as yesterday taught, agreeing is where the story starts. Gellius says he found the answer satisfying. The philosopher had been pale. He hadn't said yes.
screen: `EVEN THE WISE FLINCH.` · `SENECA'S FIRST MOVEMENTS.` · `THE JOLT, THE YES, THE RUNAWAY.` · `YOU DECIDE WHETHER TO AGREE.` · then, large: `THE JOLT ISN'T ME.`

segments.voice: Remember one jolt from the past day or two. A sharp noise, a rude message, a near miss. Feel for where it landed in your body, the chest, the stomach, the jaw. Let that echo be there. Now notice the space right after it, before the story. Breathe into that space. It's small. It's also where you live. The bell holds the time.
The first jolt. Seneca's first movement: the involuntary flinch that comes before anger or fear, and isn't yet either one. Today's word.
Your line: the jolt isn't me. The next time something jolts you today, pause for one breath before you agree with it. Day two hundred eighty-six.

287.title: Good feelings
287.hook: the Stoics kept joy, wise wishing and caution
287.howItsDone: Modern Stoic practitioners distinguish calm joy from excited pleasure and caution from fear, and try to cultivate the steady versions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first jolt, the flinch that comes before anger or fear. Your line was the jolt isn't me. Did you catch the pause before the yes? Day two hundred eighty-seven.
screen: `THE FIRST JOLT — THE JOLT ISN'T ME.`

segments.voice: After a week of this, you might be picturing the Stoic as someone with the joy dialed down to zero. Character is the only good. Comforts are just preferred. Feelings have judgments hiding in them. Check the jolt before you agree. It can start to sound like a person who never laughs at a wedding. But the Stoics had a word for the feelings they wanted more of. Not fewer feelings. Better ones. Today, the last day of our week back on the porch: eupatheia.
screen: `JOY DIALED DOWN TO ZERO?` → `NOT FEWER FEELINGS.` → `BETTER ONES.`

segments.voice: Eupatheia is Greek: eu, good or well, plus pathos, the word we met two days ago. So, good feelings. Diogenes Laërtius reports that the Stoics named three, and each one is the healthy twin of a passion. Instead of giddy, grasping pleasure, there's joy: a calm, deep gladness at what's truly good. Instead of craving, there's wishing, wanting something wisely and in the right measure. And instead of fear, there's caution: sensible care about real dangers, like looking both ways without panicking about the traffic. Notice there are three twins for four passions. There's no good version of distress for the fully wise person, because the Stoics thought such a person had nothing truly bad to grieve over. That's one of their hardest claims, and we'll be honest about it in two weeks. Seneca has a lovely line on this in a letter to his friend Lucilius. He says, roughly, believe me, real joy is a serious thing. He means it isn't a sugar rush; it's steady, it comes from inside, and it doesn't vanish when the party ends. The same report lists finer kinds under each: under wishing, goodwill and warm affection; under joy, delight and cheerfulness. So look back at this week. Home to the porch. Arete, character first. The four virtues. Adiaphora, nice not needed. Pathos, and the sentence inside a feeling. The first jolt. And now the good feelings. Put together, the goal was never a cold life. It was a clear one, with room for gladness that no one can take.
screen: `EU + PATHOS: GOOD FEELINGS.` · `JOY, WISHING, CAUTION.` · `REAL JOY IS A SERIOUS THING.` · `THE WEEK ON THE PORCH.` · then, large: `JOY IS ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Look for one good feeling that's here right now, or was here today. Maybe small: gladness at the light, relief, warmth for someone, the quiet satisfaction of a task done. Find it. Now let it be exactly as big as it is. Don't inflate it, don't wave it away. Rest in it, breathing. The bell holds the time.
Eupatheia. Greek for good feelings: joy, wise wishing and caution, the healthy twins of the passions. Today's word.
Your line: joy is allowed. Notice one good feeling today and let it stay without apology. That's our week back on the porch. Next week, the Stoic world. Day two hundred eighty-seven.

what it means: Stoics kept good feelings, joy, wise wishing and caution.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius 7.116 lists chara, boulēsis and eulabeia, with no good counterpart to distress.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
